OPERATIVE NOTE DICTATED BY: Jack Blue, MD DICTATED: 6/7/2009 8:03 P 000087489 TRANSCRIBED: 6/8/2009 1:06 A vl D PATIENT NAME: Test, Ihe HEALTH RECORD NO.: 123456783 BILLING NO.: 88888888 ROOM NO.: SIC Date of Procedure: 11/28/06 PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSES: Aortic stenosis and mitral insufficiency. POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSES: Aortic stenosis and mitral insufficiency. PROCEDURE PERFORMED: Aortic valve replacement with a 21 mm Edwards Magna bovine pericardial bioprosthesis and a reverse saphenous vein graft to the right coronary. SURGEON: Dr. Blue. ASSISTANT: Pat Yellow, CST. ANESTHESIA: General tracheal anesthesia, Dr. Green. Aortic cross clamp time was 117 minutes. Cardiopulmonary bypass time was 168 minutes. Atrial and ventricular pacing wires. Drains - 32 French mediastinal chest tube, 28 French mediastinal chest tube. FINDINGS: Good saphenous vein conduit, normal ascending aorta, aortic valve was trileaflet with heavy calcification to the leaflets. The annulus was not too heavily calcified with moderate aortic annular calcification. Also noted was a right coronary ostial intimal flap that was noted after I was getting ready to seat the valve and this will be described in the text of the operation; therefore the right coronary was grafted. The right coronary was a 2.5 mm vessel with no distal disease. INDICATIONS FOR PROCEDURE: The patient is a 73-year-old woman who was found to have known aortic stenosis and found to have breast carcinoma needing resection of her breast cancer; however, has had severe aortic stenosis prior to undergoing breast cancer surgery. She needed her heart fixed. The patient is brought to the operating room for aortic valve replacement. Preoperative echocardiogram demonstrates severe aortic stenosis and moderate aortic insufficiency and 2+ mitral insufficiency. Intraoperative transesophageal echocardiogram was performed by Dr. Mauve. DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCEDURE: The patient was brought to the operating room and placed in a comfortable supine position on the operating table. She underwent induction of general endotracheal anesthesia and placement of invasive monitor, lines and intraoperative echocardiogram by Dr. Mauve. Echocardiogram demonstrated severe aortic stenosis and heavily calcified leaflets with moderate mitral insufficiency given her age. It was my impression that decompressing her outflow tract would improve her mitral valve insufficiency. The patient was then positioned, prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. A median sternotomy was accomplished. The chest was opened and a mediastinal dissection proceeded. The pericardium was opened and suspended. The patient was heparinized. The distal ascending aorta was cannulated through double aortic pursestring sutures. A two stage venous cannula was positioned to the right atrial appendage pursestring and the patient was initiated on cardiopulmonary bypass. Antegrade and retrograde cardioplegia cannulas were positioned. An LV sump cannula was positioned through right superior pulmonary vein. The patient was cooled to 32 degrees centigrade. The aorta was cross clamped and antegrade and retrograde cold blood cardioplegia was administered. After diastolic rest of the heart we made a transverse aortotomy with a hockey stick extension down into the noncoronary sinus. Exposure of the valve was actually pretty descent. Valve findings as noted previously. The valve was sharply excised. The majority of the annular debridement was done fortunately with the scissors; i.e., the majority of the annular calcifications were in the leaflets and not so much in the annulus. Once we got the leaflets cut out the annulus was d brided of the remainder of the calcific debris. I incised it prior to placement of sutures and it sized out to 21 mm sized out very easily and in fact a 23 almost fit. I then placed multiple annular sutures circumferentially about the annulus that was consistent with interrupted 2-0 Ethibond horizontal mattress pledgeted sutures with pledgets on the ventricular side. Once we got all our sutures in, I resized the 21 mm sizer. A 21 interannular sizer was quit snug; however, the sizer on the supra-annular position looked quite comfortable. A 21 mm valve was brought up to the field and it was washed and then brought to operative field. While I was examining the root of the heart I noted that there an intimal dissection of the ostium of the right coronary that is completely unexplainable. There was no direct cannulation of the right coronary ostium. There was no mechanical debridement at the right coronary ostium but fortuitously identified the right coronary intimal tear and it was an intimal tear of the aortic wall and it extended to the right coronary ostium. I tacked this intima down to the aortic wall with interrupted horizontal mattress 5-0 Prolene suture but I was very uncomfortable just simply leaving this in place that it posed the possibility for acute right coronary dissection, RV infarct, and inferior wall infarct postoperatively. Therefore, even though she did not have any coronary disease, I was very concerned about leaving her with an unprotected right coronary. I therefore asked Pat Yellow, my assistant, to scrub and take a segment of vein from the left lower leg greater saphenous vein was harvested and the wound was closed in layers with absorbable suture. While she was taking vein, I placed annular sutures through the valve, sewing ring the valve and then seated down into the annulus and it seated nicely. It was seated first in the left coronary sinus followed by the right coronary sinus followed by the noncoronary sinus. The remainder of the sutures was tied circumferentially. I examined the valve and it appeared to be seated well and I was very pleased with the seating. Pat Yellow was still procuring vein when I was closing the aortotomy. The aortotomy was closed in a two layer fashion with running 4-0 Prolene in a two layer fashion. The first layer was a running horizontal mattress with 4-0 Prolene followed by over and over 4-0 Prolene. By this time the vein was out. I identified a spot in the mid right coronary about the level of the acute margin, made an arteriotomy and sewed the vein graft end-to-side with running 7-0 Prolene suture. I made a single 4.4 mm aortotomy distal to my transverse aortotomy and anastomosed the vein graft end-to-side with running 5-0 Prolene suture. The patient was rewarmed while I reconstructed the last anastomosis and a warm dose of cardioplegia was given through the retrograde cannula. The patient was positioned in Trendelenburg position. The ventricle and aorta were de-aired out the ascending aorta. The patient was positioned head down position. The aortic cross clamp was removed. The patient's rhythm returned to ventricular fibrillation. I defibrillated the heart several times with loading dose of Lidocaine and amiodarone and was finally able to get her defibrillated to a paced rhythm. The graft was de-aired and the bulldog was released. The aortotomy was hemostatic. Atrial and ventricular pacing wires were positioned and mediastinal drains were positioned and proximal graft markers were positioned. With satisfactory reperfusion time, we went ahead and ventilated the patient, removed the retrograde cannula was previously removed. The LV sump cannula was removed once I had the heart beating. We then proceeded with echocardiogram interrogation. Echocardiogram interrogation demonstrated satisfactory de-airing and satisfactory valve function with no aortic insufficiency and only trivial mitral insufficiency. With that result, we removed the antegrade cardioplegia needle and then weaned and separated from cardiopulmonary bypass on low dose inotropic support. The venous cannula was removed. The pump line was administered through the aortic cannula with satisfactory hemodynamics. Protamine was administered. We gained hemostasis through the mediastinum. The aorta was de-cannulated. Pursestring sutures were secured. With satisfactory hemostasis we preceded closure. The sternum was approximated with interrupted #7 stainless steel wires. The deep fascia was closed with running #1 PDS. The subcutaneous tissue was closed with 2-0 Vicryl. The skin edges were closed with 3-0 Monocryl. The patient's wounds were dressed in a dry, sterile dressing. The patient tolerated the procedure well with no operative complications. The patient was returned to the surgical intensive care unit in critical condition. ___________________________ Jack Blue, MD cc: Donald M Red, MD Jack Blue, MD Chip Orange, MD DOCUMENT #: 2487825 1

                     breast carcinoma needing resection of her breast cancer; 
                     however, has had severe aortic stenosis prior to undergoing 
                     breast cancer surgery.  She needed her heart fixed.  The 
                     patient is brought to the operating room for aortic valve 
                     replacement.  Preoperative echocardiogram demonstrates severe 
                     aortic stenosis and moderate aortic insufficiency and 2+ 
                     mitral insufficiency.  Intraoperative transesophageal 
                     echocardiogram was performed by Dr. Mauve. 
                      
                     DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCEDURE: The patient was brought to the 
                     operating room and placed in a comfortable supine position on 
                     the operating table.  She underwent induction of general 
                     endotracheal anesthesia and placement of invasive monitor, 
                     lines and intraoperative echocardiogram by Dr. Mauve. 
                     Echocardiogram demonstrated severe aortic stenosis and heavily 
                     calcified leaflets with moderate mitral insufficiency given 
                     her age.  It was my impression that decompressing her outflow 
                     tract would improve her mitral valve insufficiency.  The 
                     patient was then positioned, prepped and draped in the usual 
                     sterile fashion.  A median sternotomy was accomplished.  The 
                     chest was opened and a mediastinal dissection proceeded. The 
                     pericardium was opened and suspended. The patient was 
                     heparinized.  The distal ascending aorta was cannulated 
                     through double aortic pursestring sutures.  A two stage venous 
                     cannula was positioned to the right atrial appendage 
                     pursestring and the patient was initiated on cardiopulmonary 
                     bypass.  Antegrade and retrograde cardioplegia cannulas were 
                     positioned.  An LV sump cannula was positioned through right 
                     superior pulmonary vein.  The patient was cooled to 32 degrees 
                     centigrade. The aorta was cross clamped and antegrade and 
                     retrograde cold blood cardioplegia was administered.  After 
                     diastolic rest of the heart we made a transverse aortotomy 
                     with a hockey stick extension down into the noncoronary sinus. 
                     Exposure of the valve was actually pretty descent. Valve 
                     findings as noted previously. The valve was sharply excised. 
                     The majority of the annular debridement was done fortunately 
                     with the scissors; i.e., the majority of the annular 
                     calcifications were in the leaflets and not so much in the 
                     annulus.  Once we got the leaflets cut out the annulus was d 
                     brided of the remainder of the calcific debris. I incised it 
                     prior to placement of sutures and it sized out to 21 mm sized 
                     out very easily and in fact a 23 almost fit. I then placed 
                     multiple annular sutures circumferentially about the annulus 
                     that was consistent with interrupted 2-0 Ethibond horizontal 
                     mattress pledgeted sutures with pledgets on the ventricular 
                     side.  Once we got all our sutures in, I resized the 21 mm 
                     sizer.  A 21 interannular sizer was quit snug; however, the 
                     sizer on the supra-annular position looked quite comfortable. 
                     A 21 mm valve was brought up to the field and it was washed 
                     and then brought to operative field.  While I was examining 
                     the root of the heart I noted that there an intimal dissection 
                     of the ostium of the right coronary that is completely 
                     unexplainable. There was no direct cannulation of the right 
                     coronary ostium.  There was no mechanical debridement at the 
                     right coronary ostium but fortuitously identified the right 
                     coronary intimal tear and it was an intimal tear of the aortic 
                     wall and it extended to the right coronary ostium.  I tacked 
                     this intima down to the aortic wall with interrupted 
                     horizontal mattress 5-0 Prolene suture but I was very 
                     uncomfortable just simply leaving this in place that it posed 
                     the possibility for acute right coronary dissection, RV 
                     infarct, and inferior wall infarct postoperatively. Therefore, 
                     even though she did not have any coronary disease, I was very 
                     concerned about leaving her with an unprotected right 
                     coronary.  I therefore asked Pat Yellow, my assistant, 
                     to scrub and take a segment of vein from the left lower leg 
                     greater saphenous vein was harvested and the wound was closed 
                     in layers with absorbable suture.  While she was taking vein, 
                     I placed annular sutures through the valve, sewing ring the 
                     valve and then seated down into the annulus and it seated 
                     nicely.  It was seated first in the left coronary sinus 
                     followed by the right coronary sinus followed by the 
                     noncoronary sinus.  The remainder of the sutures was tied 
                     circumferentially.  I examined the valve and it appeared to be 
                     seated well and I was very pleased with the seating. 
                     Pat Yellow was still procuring vein when I was closing 
                     the aortotomy.  The aortotomy was closed in a two layer 
                     fashion with running 4-0 Prolene in a two layer fashion.  The 
                     first layer was a running horizontal mattress with 4-0 Prolene 
                     followed by over and over 4-0 Prolene.  By this time the vein 
                     was out.  I identified a spot in the mid right coronary about 
                     the level of the acute margin, made an arteriotomy and sewed 
                     the vein graft end-to-side with running 7-0 Prolene suture.  I 
                     made a single 4.4 mm aortotomy distal to my transverse 
                     aortotomy and anastomosed the vein graft end-to-side with 
                     running 5-0 Prolene suture.  The patient was rewarmed while I 
                     reconstructed the last anastomosis and a warm dose of 
                     cardioplegia was given through the retrograde cannula.  The 
                     patient was positioned in Trendelenburg position. The 
                     ventricle and aorta were de-aired out the ascending aorta. 
                     The patient was positioned head down position.  The aortic 
                     cross clamp was removed.  The patient's rhythm returned to 
                     ventricular fibrillation.  I defibrillated the heart several 
                     times with loading dose of Lidocaine and amiodarone and was 
                     finally able to get her defibrillated to a paced rhythm.  The 
                     graft was de-aired and the bulldog was released.  The 
                     aortotomy was hemostatic. Atrial and ventricular pacing wires 
                     were positioned and mediastinal drains were positioned and 
                     proximal graft markers were positioned.  With satisfactory 
                     reperfusion time, we went ahead and ventilated the patient, 
                     removed the retrograde cannula was previously removed.  The LV 
                     sump cannula was removed once I had the heart beating.  We 
                     then proceeded with echocardiogram interrogation. 
                     Echocardiogram interrogation demonstrated satisfactory 
                     de-airing and satisfactory valve function with no aortic 
                     insufficiency and only trivial mitral insufficiency.  With 
                     that result, we removed the antegrade cardioplegia needle and 
                     then weaned and separated from cardiopulmonary bypass on low 
                     dose inotropic support.  The venous cannula was removed. The 
                     pump line was administered through the aortic cannula with 
                     satisfactory hemodynamics.  Protamine was administered.  We 
                     gained hemostasis through the mediastinum.  The aorta was 
                     de-cannulated.  Pursestring sutures were secured. With 
                     satisfactory hemostasis we preceded closure.  The sternum was 
                     approximated with interrupted #7 stainless steel wires.  The 
                     deep fascia was closed with running #1 PDS.  The subcutaneous 
                     tissue was closed with 2-0 Vicryl. The skin edges were closed 
                     with 3-0 Monocryl.  The patient's wounds were dressed in a 
                     dry, sterile dressing.  The patient tolerated the procedure 
                     well with no operative complications.  The patient was 
                     returned to the surgical intensive care unit in critical 
                     condition.
